passage: Last week Vijay called me "Speedy Gonzales" because I run fast in PT class. I laughed so hard my water bottle fell. Then he did it again at lunch, and I laughed again, and Vijay did a little bow. It felt like our secret club joke. But when Rohan from the next bench said, "Preeti, why is your lunchbox always the same dal-roti?" I went quiet and stared at the steel dabba. Rohan kept grinning and repeated it. Vijay noticed my face before I said anything. He said, "Arre Rohan, that's not funny, stop." I still felt hot in my ears. I'm not sure whether Rohan meant harm.

qa.q: What nickname did Vijay give Preeti in PT class?
qa.a: Vijay called Preeti "Speedy Gonzales" for running fast in PT class.

qa.q: What was Preeti feeling when Rohan asked about the lunchbox, and what else might explain the silence?
qa.a: Most likely Preeti felt embarrassed and hurt, shown by going quiet, staring at the dabba and the hot ears. Preeti might also have been unsure how to answer, since Rohan was grinning and may not have meant harm.

qa.q: What could Preeti try next time someone teases about something sore?
qa.a: Preeti could say calmly, "I don't like that joke," or tell Vijay or a teacher afterwards. Speaking up early makes it easier for the teaser to stop.

qa.q: How might Rohan see the lunchbox comment, compared with Preeti?
qa.a: Rohan may think it was harmless banter like Vijay's nickname, so Rohan keeps grinning. Rohan may not realise the topic was a sore spot for Preeti until seeing Preeti's quiet face.

grounding: Shows the same teasing style as fun with Vijay (both laugh, safe topic) and hurtful with Rohan (sore spot, continues after silence).

passage: Teacher's note, Class 5. During the group activity today Zainab and Rehana were paired. Rehana kept saying "Zainab the sleepy tortoise" about her slow start, and both girls giggled, so I let it pass. Later a third child added a comment about Zainab's stammer while reading aloud. Zainab looked at her shoes, her smile went flat, and she stopped taking part. The other child continued for a few seconds. I walked over, asked Zainab quietly whether she wanted to step outside with me, and reminded the group that jokes stop when someone goes quiet. I will check in with Zainab tomorrow and speak with the other child privately. 🙂

qa.q: Who was paired for the group activity in Class 5?
qa.a: Zainab and Rehana were paired for the group activity.

qa.q: What did Zainab's flat smile and looking at her shoes suggest she felt, and what else could it mean?
qa.a: It most likely suggests she felt hurt or embarrassed about the comment on her stammer. It could also mean she was tired or overwhelmed, so the teacher checks in rather than assuming.

qa.q: What could the teacher do to support Zainab after this?
qa.a: The teacher can check in with Zainab tomorrow, speak privately with the child who made the comment, and keep reminding the class that jokes stop when someone goes quiet.

qa.q: Why might Rehana's tortoise joke feel different to Zainab than the stammer comment?
qa.a: Zainab laughed along with Rehana's joke, so it felt shared and safe. The stammer comment pointed at something she may already feel sensitive about.

grounding: Contrasts affectionate teasing where both laugh with teasing that hit a sore spot and continued after distress, with a teacher checking in.

passage:
Tuesday night.
Today at lunch my best friend Payal called me "Professor Glasses" again. Usually I laugh, because she only says it when I win the quiz, and I call her "Speedy Noodle" because she finishes her tiffin in two minutes. We both crack up.
But this morning the eye doctor told Mummy I need thicker lenses, and a few boys were already sniggering at my new frames. Payal said it loudly and pushed my specs up my nose.
I didn't laugh. I just looked at my dal.
She kept grinning for a second, then stopped. "Hey. Too much?"
I nodded.
She said sorry and never said it again all afternoon. On the bus she gave me half her mango slice.
Maybe tomorrow it will feel funny again. Not yet.
- Manoj

qa.q: What nickname did Payal call Manoj at lunch?
qa.a: She called Manoj "Professor Glasses" again.

qa.q: What was Manoj most likely feeling when the nickname came up today, and what else could the silence mean?
qa.a: Manoj most likely felt hurt and embarrassed, because the joke came on the same day as the thicker lenses and the boys' sniggering. The silence could also have been plain tiredness, which is why asking was better than guessing.

qa.q: Which choice of Payal's worked, and why?
qa.a: Stopping mid-grin to ask "Too much?" worked, because it gave Manoj a chance to say yes and the teasing ended before it hurt more.

qa.q: How might Payal have seen the joke differently from Manoj today?
qa.a: To Payal it was the same friendly nickname as always, tied to quiz wins; she probably did not know the new lenses had turned it into a sore spot until Manoj went quiet.

grounding: The diary shows a shared nickname that is usually affectionate becoming hurtful when it touches a fresh sore spot, and the friend checking in once the narrator goes quiet.

passage:
On the dusty ground behind the panchayat office, the boys played cricket until the sun turned orange. Madhav bowled; Sahil swung and missed.
"Arre Sahil, you bat like a buffalo chasing a fly!" Madhav shouted. Sahil laughed and swished the bat behind him like a tail.
Then Madhav flapped his arms and fell sideways into the dust, copying how Sahil had tumbled off his cycle at the temple fair while half the village watched. The other boys hooted.
Sahil's grin went flat. He picked at the tape on the bat handle and said nothing.
Madhav began a second fall, saw Sahil's face, and stopped halfway. He dusted his knees and walked over. "The fair thing still bad?"
Sahil shrugged, then nodded once.
"Okay. Buffalo only, no cycle," Madhav said, and Sahil gave a small smile.

qa.q: What did Madhav copy that made the other boys hoot?
qa.a: Madhav copied how Sahil had tumbled off his cycle at the temple fair.

qa.q: How can you tell Sahil felt differently about the two jokes?
qa.a: Sahil laughed and played along with the buffalo joke, but after the cycle fall his grin went flat and he picked at the tape in silence, which suggests he felt embarrassed and hurt. He might also have been tired, which is why Madhav asked.

qa.q: What small step helped turn things around?
qa.a: Madhav stopped halfway through the second fall and asked a short, direct question, then dropped the sore joke and kept the one Sahil enjoyed.

qa.q: If you were one of the boys who hooted, what might you notice next time?
qa.a: You might notice that Sahil laughed at one joke and went silent at the other, and that hooting along can keep a painful memory going.

grounding: The village cricket scene contrasts a safe shared joke with one that hits a sore memory, and shows the teaser stopping to check when the friend goes quiet.

passage:
Rosa and Freya walked home through the park in Leeds, kicking wet leaves.
"Your hat looks like a tea cosy," Rosa said, and Freya laughed so hard she snorted.
"Your wellies look like two frogs," Freya shot back. They were both giggling.
Then Rosa sang, "Tea Cosy Girl, do the solo you messed up!"
Freya's laugh stopped. She tugged the hat lower and walked faster, eyes on the path.
Rosa hurried to catch up. "Hey. Was that a bad one? I'll stop."
Freya was quiet for a few steps. "The solo thing, yeah. Mrs Hale sighed at me in front of the whole choir."
"Sorry. That's off the list," Rosa said.
Freya bumped her shoulder. "The tea cosy can stay, though." 🙂

qa.q: What did Freya say Rosa's wellies looked like?
qa.a: Two frogs.

qa.q: What was Freya feeling when Rosa mentioned the solo, and what is one other reading of her walking faster?
qa.a: Freya most likely felt embarrassed and stung, since Mrs Hale had sighed at her in front of the choir. Walking faster could also have meant she was simply cold or wanted to get home, so Rosa's question was the way to find out.

qa.q: What went right after the joke landed badly?
qa.a: Rosa noticed the change, caught up, asked instead of guessing, and promised to drop the solo joke, while the safe hat joke stayed as a shared laugh.

qa.q: How might the walk have ended if Rosa had kept singing?
qa.a: Freya would probably have felt mocked about a real embarrassment, and a fun walk could have turned into a hurtful one.

grounding: Two friends trade safe, affectionate insults until one joke touches a sore spot, and the teaser checks in when her friend goes quiet.

passage: In the hostel dining hall, Vandana balanced a chapati on her head. "Aditi snores like a pressure cooker. Whistle, whistle!" Aditi laughed and flicked a pea at her. "And you talk in your sleep about mangoes." They both giggled. Then Vandana added, "Maybe that's why you failed the Hindi test. Too tired from whistling." Aditi's smile dropped. She looked down and pushed her dal around without eating. Vandana noticed the silence and put the chapati down. "Hey. That one wasn't funny, was it? Sorry." Aditi shrugged, then said quietly, "I studied for that test." Vandana nodded. "Want to practise together after prep?" After a moment, Aditi slid the pickle jar across to her.

qa.q: What did Vandana say Aditi snores like?
qa.a: A pressure cooker.

qa.q: What might Aditi's pushing her dal around suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: Most likely hurt and embarrassed, because the Hindi test was a sore spot. She might also just have been tired, but the sudden silence after the joke points to hurt.

qa.q: What did Vandana get right once Aditi went quiet?
qa.a: She noticed the silence, stopped the joke, said plainly that it wasn't funny, apologised and offered to practise together.

qa.q: What would change if Vandana had kept joking about the test?
qa.a: Aditi would likely feel mocked rather than teased, and the trust that made the snoring joke fun could have been damaged.

grounding: It illustrates teasing that is affectionate while both laugh and turns hurtful when it hits a sore spot, and a friend checking in when the other goes quiet.
